# Box

```{r}
#| include: false
source("../R/setup.R")
```

How is each group spread out? `box` draws a **box plot** for each group, a
summary of the measured column.
A box spans the lower quartile to the upper, with a line at the median. Whiskers
reach to the most extreme values *within 1.5 times the interquartile range (IQR)
of the box*. Any values beyond that limit are outliers, drawn individually as
dots. `bar * mean` gives only one number per group, while `box` shows how the
whole group is spread. An [`interval`](interval.qmd) needs a transform to supply
its low and high values, while a box computes its whole summary itself. Boxes
are vertical when the categories are on `x` and horizontal when they are on
`y`; see [Horizontal boxes](#horizontal-boxes).

The construction is John Tukey's, from *Exploratory Data Analysis* [@tukey1977].
His book gives two versions. The **box-and-whisker plot** runs its whiskers to
the smallest and largest values, as Mary Eleanor Spear's **range bar**
[@spear1952] had done a quarter century earlier, in 1952. The **schematic
plot** stops them at a **fence**, 1.5 times the length of the box beyond each
end of the box. Each value beyond a fence is drawn on its own, as an outlier.
Readers kept the first name, now usually shortened to box plot. Most software,
gog included, gives that name to the schematic plot and draws it by default.

There is one difference from his book. Tukey's box spans **hinges**. Sort the
values and cut the sorted list in half; when the count is odd, the middle value
belongs to both halves. Take the median of each half: those two medians are the
hinges. gog spans the lower and upper quartiles instead, as most software does.
The two agree when a group has an odd number of values, and can differ slightly
when the number is even. For the four values 1, 2, 3 and 4, the hinges are 1.5
and 3.5, while gog's box runs from 1.75 to 3.25.

## A summary per group {#a-summary-per-group}

How do the three species differ in petal length, not only on average but in how
widely each varies? The `iris_flowers` table holds 150 iris flowers, 50 of each
of three species, measured in centimeters. Put the categorical column,
`species`, on `x`, and put the measured column, `petal_length`, on `y`. The mark
computes the summary itself:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(iris_flowers)
```

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + box + x(species) + y(petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Distribution of petal length per species")
```

*"Given the iris flowers: boxes, x is species, y is petal length."*

Every box is built the same way. About half the flowers of a species fall
inside the box, the middle 50% from the lower quartile to the upper. The line across the
box is the median. Each whisker runs from the box to the most extreme value
inside the fence. The separate dots are the outliers: flowers more than 1.5
times the IQR from the box. The whisker stops before them, and each one is
drawn on its own.

## Distribution across many groups {#distribution-across-many-groups}

Which continent's countries differ most in life expectancy, and which
countries fall far below the rest of their own continent? Five boxes
answer both, and you read each one exactly as you read the species boxes. The
`gapminder_2007` table holds one row for each of 142 countries in 2007. The
plot shows their life expectancy by continent, five distributions in one panel,
and each outlier is one country:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gapminder_2007)
```

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + box + x(continent) + y(life) +
  x_label("Continent") + y_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("Life expectancy by continent, 2007")
```

Africa's box is the tallest, so the middle half of its countries is the most
spread out. From its lowest value to its highest, Asia covers the widest
range, but only because of one country far below the rest. The low dot below Asia is Afghanistan, and the one
below the Americas is Haiti. Each is far enough below its continent's box that
no whisker reaches it. That is what Tukey's construction is for: the box and
whiskers cover the ordinary values, and the dots mark the unusual ones.

## Horizontal boxes {#horizontal-boxes}

When the category names are long, or there are many of them, the boxes should
be horizontal. Swap the two positions, and the plot is drawn with its axes
exchanged. gog has no word like ggplot2's `coord_flip()`, because it would be a
second way to say the same thing. gog reads the two bindings
and decides from them which axis carries the numbers, exactly as
[`bar`](bar.qmd) does.

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + box + x(life) + y(continent) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + y_label("Continent") +
  title("The same five distributions, horizontal")
```

Compare it with the vertical version in [Distribution across many
groups](#distribution-across-many-groups). Every box, whisker and outlier dot
keeps its place relative to its neighbors. Only the two axes have changed
places. Afghanistan and Haiti are still the two dots beyond their continents'
whiskers. Everything later in this chapter works the same on either axis: the
whisker rule, the color split, `dodge` and `style()`.

The swap matters most when the names are long. The `tenure` table is invented:
five teams, thirty people in each, and the years each person has been at the
company. Each category takes a **slot**, the stretch of the axis that belongs
to one category. With the categories on `x`, each name has the width of one
slot, and if any name is wider, gog turns every name to read upward. With the
categories on `y`, as below, each name is written in full on one line:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(tenure)
```

```{r}
data(tenure) + box + x(years) + y(team) +
  x_label("Years at the company") +
  title("Team names fit on a vertical axis")
```

A box needs a continuous column to summarize, so two categorical axes are
refused, exactly as they are on a bar. [What it refuses](#what-it-refuses)
shows that refusal.

## Whiskers to the extremes {#whiskers-to-the-extremes}

Sometimes you do not want outliers drawn separately. You want the whiskers to
run to the true minimum and maximum. The box then shows the **five-number
summary**: the minimum, the lower quartile, the median, the upper quartile and
the maximum. The mark takes one **parameter** for this, a named option inside
its parentheses: `box(whiskers = "range")`:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + box(whiskers = "range") + x(continent) + y(life) +
  x_label("Continent") + y_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("The same, with whiskers to the full range")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: boxes with whiskers to the range, x is continent, y is
life."*

Now Afghanistan and Haiti are the ends of their whiskers rather than dots, and
no value is drawn as an outlier. The default is `"tukey"`: fences and outliers,
the standard box plot. `"range"` draws the whole five-number summary.
`whiskers` is not a setting, because it changes the summary itself: which
values the whiskers reach. A setting changes only how the summary looks, such
as its color or line width; those are in [What you can set](#what-you-can-set).

## Why `box` needs no transform {#why-box-needs-no-transform}

An [`interval`](interval.qmd) cannot draw without a transform to give it a low
and a high. A `box` never needs one. An `interval` is only a shape, a span from
a low value to a high one. *Which* low and high it spans is a real choice: a
min–max range, a confidence interval, or a pre-computed pair. A `box` always
draws the same kind of summary: quartiles, a median and whiskers. Only the
whisker rule can change, through the mark's own `whiskers`. A statistic that is
always drawn by the same mark belongs inside that mark, not in a separate
transform. So the shortest sentence that draws a box is `box + x + y`, with no
transform. Adding any transform other than `dodge` is refused, and the message
says what to write instead, as [What it refuses](#what-it-refuses) shows.

The same principle keeps the [channel
vocabulary](../grammar.qmd#channels-a-column-made-visible) small: something that
only one mark can use belongs inside that mark, not in the shared vocabulary.
Taking ggplot2's `ymin`, `lower`, `middle`, `upper` and `ymax` as channels
would add five channels. Three of them, `lower`, `middle` and `upper`, would
mean something only on a box. Instead the summary is computed inside the
mark, and the channel vocabulary does not grow.

The table below sets the four marks side by side. Three of them read a low and
a high value from a transform, and `box` computes its own summary:

| Mark | The spread it draws |
|---|---|
| `interval * range` | a whisker from the low value to the high |
| `ribbon * range` | the band between the two values, filled |
| `line * range` | the two values as two separate strokes |
| `box` | quartiles, median and whiskers, with no transform to write |

`box` is also one of several marks that draw a distribution, and each answers a
different question. [`bar * bin`](bar.qmd) draws one variable's histogram: how
many values fall in each bin? [`interval`](interval.qmd) draws a range or
an error bar: between which two values do a group's values fall? `box` gives the
summary per group: where are its middle half, its median and its unusual
values? The violin
([`ribbon * density`](ribbon.qmd#the-violin-a-distribution-per-category))
draws an estimate of the whole distribution that summary is computed from: where
are the values dense, and where are they sparse? An interval can also span the
box's two quartiles:
`interval * range(0.25, 0.75)` draws the same middle half, as [A band between
two quantiles](../transforms.qmd#a-band-between-two-quantiles) shows.

## Coloring the boxes {#coloring-the-boxes}

The three species boxes in [A summary per group](#a-summary-per-group) are all
one color, so only the species names on the axis identify each box. A color per species lets
a reader match each box to the same species in another plot. A color also
splits each slot by a second category, such as an era. `color` gives each box
its own hue, and adds one legend that names the hues. It is the same categorical
split that `bar` and `interval` make. Here `color` is mapped to the same column
as `x`, so it colors one box per group:

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + box + x(species) + y(petal_length) + color(species) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("The same distributions, colored by species")
```

*"Given the iris flowers: boxes, x is species, y is petal length, color by
species."*

Mapping `color` to a *second* category splits each category on x into one box
per color. Without `dodge` those boxes are drawn at the same x and overlap.
Their fills turn translucent so each stays readable, as the upper plot in
[Transforms it takes](#transforms-it-takes) shows.
[`dodge`](../transforms.qmd#dodge-side-by-side-instead-of-on-top) sets them
side by side, as the plot below does for each continent's two eras. The
`gm_eras` table holds the Gapminder countries in 1957 and in 2007, one row for
each country and year, and `era` names the year:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gm_eras)
```

```{r}
data(gm_eras) + box * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + color(era) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Life expectancy per continent, 1957 vs 2007")
```

*"Given the gapminder eras: boxes derived by dodge, x is continent, y is life,
color by era."*

In every continent, the 2007 box is entirely above the 1957 box. Oceania's 1957
box looks like a flat line. Its two countries differed by only 0.07 years, so a
box spanning the middle half of their values has almost no height. If every
value in a group's middle half were the same, the box would have no height at
all. gog does not give it a minimum height to make the spread look larger.

`color`, `pattern` and `group` can each split the rows of one category into
several boxes, as on a bar or an interval. `size` and `opacity` cannot be mapped to any column,
not even a category: a box takes one line width and one opacity for the whole
layer. `style(size = )` sets the width of every line a box draws. That covers
the outline, the whiskers and the caps (the short lines across the whisker
ends). The median is one pixel thicker.

## Transforms it takes {#transforms-it-takes}

A transform computes new values from the rows, and the mark draws those values
instead of the rows. The table lists, by kind, the transforms a box takes and
the ones it refuses:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
mark_transforms("box")
```

A box takes only one transform, `dodge`, so one figure shows it. The figure
shows the same boxes twice, first without `dodge` and then with it.

**Collision modifiers.** Collision modifiers move marks that would be drawn on
top of one another. When a split draws
several boxes at one place, `dodge` sets them side by side, and it changes
nothing in their summaries. Here the split is `color(era)`, which gives two
boxes for each continent, one for 1957 and one for 2007. Without `dodge`, as in
the upper plot, the two boxes share one place, so they overlap and their fills
turn translucent. With `dodge`, each box takes its own half of the slot:

```{r}
((data(gm_eras) + box + x(continent) + y(life) + color(era) + title("box")) /
   (data(gm_eras) + box * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + color(era) +
      title("box * dodge"))) +
  theme(height = 800)
```

*"Given the gapminder eras: boxes, x is continent, y is life, color by era,
above boxes derived by dodge, x is continent, y is life, color by era."*

Each box marks the same quartiles, median and whiskers in both plots. Only its
place and its width change: the two boxes share the slot, so each is half as
wide.

A box refuses every transform in the Refuses column above. It computes its own
summary, as [Why `box` needs no transform](#why-box-needs-no-transform)
explains, so it refuses the counts, the summaries and the pairs. For the same
reason it refuses the fitted lines and the running total. A
[`point`](point.qmd), a [`bar`](bar.qmd) or a [`line`](line.qmd) draws the
counts, the summaries, the fitted lines and the running total.
[`interval`](interval.qmd), [`ribbon`](ribbon.qmd), [`line`](line.qmd) and
[`step`](step.qmd) draw the pairs. Of the collision modifiers, a box takes only
`dodge`. A box's position on the axis that carries the numbers is set by its
values. Piling one box on another would move its quartiles away from the values
they mark. `stack` piles up bars, areas
and the dots of a dot plot. `jitter` moves each point a short way along the
categorical axis, and `repel` moves [`text`](text.qmd) labels. `partition`,
`flow` and `cluster` lay out rectangles, bands and branches, which
[`zone`](zone.qmd), [`ribbon`](ribbon.qmd) and [`path`](path.qmd) draw.
`layout` places a network, which [`point`](point.qmd), [`text`](text.qmd) and
[`edge`](edge.qmd) draw.

## What you can set {#what-you-can-set}

A setting changes how every box looks without reading a column, and each mark
takes its own. [Setting vs mapping](../style.qmd) shows how a setting differs from mapping a
column. These are a box's settings, with the values each accepts:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
mark_options("box")
```

`border_color` and `border_size` are useful on a box in particular, because a
box draws lines *and* a fill. The lines are the outline, the whiskers, the caps
and the median. `border_color` gives them a color of their own; without it,
they take the fill's color, so the median barely shows against the fill. A pale
fill with a dark border keeps the median easy to see. `border_size` sets the
same width as `size`, and when both are given, the box uses `border_size`.
`style(caps = FALSE)` draws the whiskers without caps, as on an
[`interval`](interval.qmd):

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + box + x(continent) + y(life) + style(caps = FALSE) +
  title("Whiskers without caps")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: boxes, x is continent, y is life, with caps off."*

`gap` sets how much of a box's slot is left empty. Unless you set it, a box
takes about half of its slot, so it is narrower than a bar. `style(gap = 0.2)`
leaves a fifth of the slot empty, as a bar does by default, so each box is as
wide as a bar:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + box + x(continent) + y(life) + style(gap = 0.2) +
  title("Boxes as wide as bars")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: boxes, x is continent, y is life, with gap 0.2."*

The boxes and their caps are wider. The quartiles, medians and whiskers mark the
same values.

`whiskers` is not in the table above, because it is a parameter, as [Whiskers
to the extremes](#whiskers-to-the-extremes) explains. A box is the one mark in
the kernel that takes a parameter. The other parameters you have met belong to
a transform, such as `bin(width = )`, or to a position, such as
`x(gdp, scale = "log")`. The plot below uses the parameter together with
settings: whiskers to the range, and a pale fill with a navy border. It reads
`gm_continents`: Asia, Europe and the Americas, measured every five years from
1952 to 2007. Each country appears twelve times, so a box here is drawn from
twelve times as many values as one drawn from gapminder 2007:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gm_continents)
```

```{r}
data(gm_continents) + box(whiskers = "range") + x(continent) + y(life) +
  style(color = "lightsteelblue", border_color = "navy", border_size = 1.2) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("Whiskers to the true extremes, and a border")
```

*"Given the gapminder continents: boxes with whiskers to the range, x is
continent, y is life, colored lightsteelblue, with border color navy and border
size 1.2."*

The navy median now shows clearly against the pale fill, and the whiskers
reach each continent's lowest and highest values.

The [grid of every mark and every setting](../style.qmd#what-you-can-set) shows
which other marks share this list. What a mark *maps* rather than sets is its
row on the [grid of marks and channels](../combinations.qmd#marks-and-channels).

## What it refuses {#what-it-refuses}

Five refusals follow. The first three concern how a box is drawn, and the last two concern what it summarizes. A dashed
`pattern` is the first. A box's `pattern` textures its fill while its lines
stay solid, so it takes a fill's texture and not a stroke's dash. `"solid"`
(the default), `"hatch"`, `"crosshatch"`, `"stripes"`, `"grid"` and `"dots"`
are accepted, and `"dashed"` is refused.

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + box + x(continent) + y(life) + style(pattern = "dashed")
```

A mapped `size` is the second. On a box, `size` is the width of the lines it
draws, and a box takes one size for the whole layer, not one per row. The
width of the box itself comes from its slot and `gap`:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + box + x(continent) + y(life) + size(life)
```

A mapped `opacity` is the third, for the same reason: a box takes one opacity
for the whole layer. Set it with `style(opacity = )` instead:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + box + x(continent) + y(life) + opacity(life)
```

Two categorical axes are the fourth. gog reads a box's two bindings to find the
axis that carries the numbers, so one axis has to be continuous. Two categories
leave a box nothing to summarize, as they leave a bar no length to draw:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + box + x(continent) + y(continent)
```

A statistic is the fifth. A box already summarizes each group into quartiles,
a median and whiskers, so the only transform it takes is `dodge`, which
computes nothing. [Why `box` needs no transform](#why-box-needs-no-transform)
gave the reason:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(iris_flowers) + box * mean + x(species) + y(petal_length)
```

The message names the fix: drop the transform, and the box draws its own
summary.

## In short {#in-short}

For each group, a box draws quartiles, a median, whiskers to the most extreme
values within 1.5 times the IQR, and a dot for each outlier. The summary
is inside the mark, so a `box` refuses every statistic and takes only `dodge`.
`whiskers` is its one parameter. Its line width and opacity are set once for
the layer. gog's box spans the quartiles, so when a group has an even number of
values it can differ slightly from Tukey's hinges.

## What comes next {#what-comes-next}

A box occupies one slot on its axis, and its width carries no value from the
table. [Ribbon](ribbon.qmd) fills the band between a low value and a high
one at every position along the axis.
